failure_modes.description: The assumption about water chemistry not promoting excessive mineral scaling is completely unsupported and unrealistic for most industrial applications
failure_modes.evidence: Real-world pipe systems almost always experience some mineral scaling, which would rapidly fill the narrow valleys between riblets, destroying both drag reduction and anti-fouling properties

failure_modes.description: The claim that hierarchical riblets will thin the viscous sublayer contradicts established fluid dynamics knowledge
failure_modes.evidence: Riblets actually work by increasing the effective surface area and reducing the cross-flow component of turbulent motion, not by thinning the viscous sublayer

failure_modes.description: The proposed drag reduction range of 4-7% is unrealistically high for industrial pipe applications
failure_modes.evidence: Published studies show riblet structures typically achieve 1-3% drag reduction in pipes, with 5% being the absolute upper limit in ideal laboratory conditions

failure_modes.description: The combination of drag reduction and anti-fouling in hierarchical structures is not novel
failure_modes.evidence: Multiple patents and publications from the past decade describe similar approaches, including US20170160821A1 and 'Bioinspired surfaces: from superhydrophobicity to self-healing' by Bhushan 2016

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis already fails its own falsification criteria
failure_modes.evidence: The falsifier states 'if biofilm adhesion strength is not reduced or if pressure drop increases' - both outcomes are highly likely given the fragile assumptions and unrealistic performance claims

failure_modes.description: The proposed solution is incompatible with real-world pipe manufacturing and installation requirements
failure_modes.evidence: Creating hierarchical structures with both micro-ridges (50-100 μm) and nano-features (1-10 μm) would be prohibitively expensive for large-diameter pipes and would likely fail during installation
